subject: Banking
title: The Facebook IPO Disaster
description: Learn The Facebook IPO Disaster in one minute.

hook.text: Facebook's 2012 IPO was the most anticipated in history. It raised $16 billion.

buildup.text: Morgan Stanley led the underwriting. They set the price at $38 per share, the maximum of the range.

discovery.text: Technical glitches on NASDAQ delayed trading. Millions of orders were stuck in limbo. The launch was chaotic.

twist.text: Morgan Stanley privately warned large investors about weak revenue while still marketing aggressively to small buyers.

climax.text: Facebook's IPO showed that hype can override fundamentals.

punchline.text: Most hyped IPO ever. Dropped 50% in three months. Hype is not value.

quiz.question: What went wrong with Facebook's IPO?
options: Overpricing, technical glitches, and uneven disclosure of revenue concerns

details.summary: Facebook's 2012 IPO at 38 dollars per share raised 16 billion dollars but was marred by a NASDAQ technical glitch, allegations that banks selectively warned large investors of reduced forecasts, and the stock dropping 50 percent within months.
details.whyItMatters: The Facebook IPO exposed how the IPO process can disadvantage retail investors. Large institutional investors received warnings about reduced revenue forecasts while everyday investors bought shares based on outdated optimistic projections.
takeaways: Facebook raised 16 billion at a 104 billion dollar valuation
NASDAQ technical failures disrupted trading on the first day
The stock fell over 50 percent before eventually recovering

faq.question: What went wrong with the Facebook IPO?
faq.answer: Three things converged: NASDAQ's systems crashed under trading volume, the offering price was set too high based on aggressive demand, and banks allegedly shared revised downward revenue estimates only with institutional investors.

faq.question: Did Facebook's IPO ultimately succeed?
faq.answer: Financially, yes. After falling 50 percent, the stock recovered within 18 months and has since grown enormously. But the initial pricing and disclosure failures cost retail investors significant short-term losses and damaged trust in the IPO process.
